newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Privatisation helps Sri Lanka plantations.
newsitem.headline: Privatisation helps Sri Lanka plantations.

text.p: Sri Lanka's plantation firms, once the mainstay of the island's economy, are again drumming up profits after privatisation and the trend is seen continuing, industry analysts said on Friday.

"Privatisation, which began in late 1992 with management and was extended to ownership in 1995, has led to reinvestment in the once debt-riddled sector," said Nandakumar Nair, head of research at brokerage John Keells.

"Sri Lanka's plantation sector is poised to recover with privatisation as investments are taking place in replanting, fertiliser and machinery, and efforts are also being made to reduce costs and raise productivity," he added.

The six listed plantation firms -- Bogawantalawa Plantations, Kotagala Plantations, Agalwatte Plantations, Kegalle Plantations, Horana Plantations and Kelani Valley Plantations -- saw their net profit rising between 50 and 500 percent in 1996.
Their shares are currently trading at an average price of 27 rupees.
Analysts expect the average price of listed plantation shares to rise to about 35 rupees in 1997 as the estates move away from just producing tea to adding value to their products.

When the government began privatising management of 23 regional plantation firms which own some 600,000 hectares of tea, rubber and coconut, they had each run up debts ranging from five million rupees to 100 million rupees.

Privatisation of ownership began in 1995 by selling 51 percent to a strategic investor and 20 percent to the public on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE). Ten percent was reserved for workers and the government retained the balance.
The strategic holding has been divested in seven more firms since last year and they are due to be floated later this year.

Ten other firms, where the process is yet to begin, are due to see strategic holdings divested between April and June, said an official of the Public Enterprise Reform Commission, which oversees privatisations.

"Since all private managers are either developing CTC (crush tea curl) tea for bags, green tea or concentrate for canned tea, we should see share prices of listed tea firms moving up to an average of about 35 rupees by the end of the year," Colin Kingsnorth, director and fund manager of Tea Plantations Investment Trust Plc (TPIT), told Reuters in Colombo.

The trust has raised $10 million on the London Stock Exchange for investing in Sri Lankan plantations that are being privatised. Kingsnorth said the trust would bid for a strategic holding in three plantation firms which are likely to be privatised in April or May.
Analysts, however, said investors were unlikely to see a repeat of the runaway growth of 1996 when the net sales average for tea was 103.88 rupees ($1.80) a kg, up from 72.21 in 1995.
High prices in 1996 were partly due to supply being affected by a severe drought in Sri Lanka.
"From here onwards growth will depend largely on the quality of the management company," said Sanjay Kulatunga, plantation sector analyst at brokerage Jardine Fleming.
Analysts also say high labour costs on Sri Lankan plantations where nearly 60 percent of the cost of production comprises wages, did not augur well for the future.
But Kingsnorth said labour costs should not prove to be a handicap as long as quality and demand for Sri Lanka tea remained high.
